## Server-driven announcements (desktop notices)

To show an announcement/warning popup in the app without shipping a release, insert a row in the `desktop_notices` table (served by `GET /api/desktop/version`). Authoring guide — markdown-only body, severities, triggers, targeting, QA previews: `docs/DESKTOP_NOTICES.md`.

## Persisted renderer state (localStorage) policy

Renderer localStorage has one ~10 MB quota, loads synchronously at boot, and keys outlive the code that wrote them — unbounded growth has frozen the renderer before (23.7 MB profile, GH #5496). Every writer must be allowlisted in `src/renderer/lib/persisted-keys/persisted-key-registry.test-data.ts` (CI fails on unregistered writers), and code review must answer three questions:

1. **What bounds it?** A cap/LRU, a TTL, reconciliation against an owning entity, or "fixed-size singleton". "It's small per write" is not a bound.
2. **Who deletes it?** New entity-keyed data belongs in SQLite; existing stores must document their deletion path or sunset plan because deletes from CLIs or other machines can bypass UI cleanup. One-shot payloads must be cleared by their consumer. Deleting a map entry means removing the key, never writing `null`.
3. **What happens when the feature dies?** Move the keys to `DEAD_KEYS` in the same PR that removes the writer; the boot sweep cleans existing profiles. Deleting the writer without registering the key strands it on user profiles forever.

Guardrail: localStorage is for small singleton UI state. Anything entity-scoped with unbounded cardinality, or payloads beyond a few KB, belongs in host-side SQLite (`@superset/local-db` schema, reached over `electronTrpc`) — localStorage collections re-serialize the whole org blob on every mutation. Since #6328 removed SQLite-backed collection persistence, every TanStack DB collection in `CollectionsProvider` is localStorage-backed, so the ~10 MB quota is shared by all of them; `withQuotaGuard`, `notifyQuotaExhausted`, and `evictInactiveOrgs` exist to absorb that pressure and are not a licence to store more.

## Verifying renderer changes via CDP

Read `.agents/skills/cdp-verification/SKILL.md`: attaching to the right renderer, repairing auth, and what counts as end-to-end evidence.

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

An installer-driven relaunch missing `SUPERSET_COMPANION_BRIDGE=1` (correct in the registry the whole time) silently gated the companion bridge off and the phone reported "Superset isn't running". The reader is PowerShell rather than `reg query` because reg.exe's console text is unparseable in principle, not merely awkward: it transcodes to the OEM codepage with best-fit substitution before the bytes reach the pipe (`™`→`T`, so a non-ASCII username corrupts JAVA_HOME), a REG_SZ containing newlines is byte-identical to two separate values (a pasted blob whose second line reads `    NODE_OPTIONS    REG_SZ    --require C:\evil.js` becomes a REAL NODE_OPTIONS in the Electron main env, spread to the host-service child), and a value may itself contain the four-space field separator. REG_SZ comes back verbatim and REG_EXPAND_SZ raw (`DoNotExpandEnvironmentNames`), so expansion happens in a second TS pass against the merged target and a same-hive `%ZBASE%` resolves whatever order the registry enumerated it in. process.env always wins; names are preserved byte-for-byte (a registry name with a leading space stays a different variable and cannot open the bridge); names are case-folded as Windows does; the read is memoized per process; `SystemRoot` unset fails loud rather than resolving powershell.exe through PATH; a read failure is `console.error`-loud and never fatal; values are NEVER logged (this key holds users' API keys, pinned by a tripwire test) | `(WIN-USER-ENV)` |

The argument held only while a next `g` actually arrived: when the agent went back to work and then blocked, crashed or was left alone, nothing replaced the card and the phone said "ready for review" for six hours about a chat that was not. USER DECISION, reversing it: retract immediately and let the companion app absorb the higher event rate. Each alert is still owed EXACTLY ONE `c`, carrying that alert's own `gx` so the phone cancels the finish it is actually holding rather than whatever card is showing; a retracted row is kept to its TTL as the cycle's dedupe record, so repeats — twenty further cycles, a session end behind a new cycle, two retirements over one in-flight send — are inert rather than a second broadcast. Because the green dot is cleared by the agent starting work again while a card may still be on the phone, the desktop also keeps a per-terminal OUTSTANDING-READY record beside its seen marks: opening a chat that is already running again reports a read for the finish that record names, the record is retired only when a host actually APPLIED the report AND only up to the generation that host acknowledged (a newer finish landing mid-report keeps its own record; a host that refused the read on its own evidence — host.db does not place that terminal in that workspace, or could not be read to check — answers `accepted: false` so the record survives for the resync to offer again), and the resync repairs the ones that were dropped — under the same cap, rotation and cooldowns as the existing repair, and never inventing one out of its own replay. Generations are ordered by a per-terminal MONOTONIC lifecycle instant (`max(now, previous+1)`, anchored on the persisted binding so it survives a restart) rather than the raw wall clock, because an NTP step-back would otherwise stamp a newer finish behind its predecessor — which the phone rejects as stale, the host cannot retract, and the renderer records as reported. Its "nothing ever existed, so send nothing" branch is bounded the same way — per terminal, against the last lifecycle instant host.db recorded before the manager started (read once at bridge start), because a wall-clock start compared against a monotonic generation lets a restart inside a backstep "prove" that an alert the previous process actually sent never existed; unreadable or absent restart evidence disables the proof rather than trusting it, since a blind `c` the phone drops is the safe failure and a swallowed retraction is not. | Windows behaviour fixes | child-process patch, cmd.exe fallback, force-foreground, watchdog, WebGL recovery, fast startup | `windows-child-process` |
| Windows user-environment merge | on Windows, `HKCU\Environment` is read through PowerShell as structured JSON and merged UNDER `process.env` at the top of the Electron main boot and BOTH host-service entries, and it replaces the login-shell snapshot entirely on win32. Upstream's snapshot spawns `%COMSPEC%` (cmd.exe) with POSIX login-shell flags (`-i -l -c`) and a POSIX body (`echo -n`, `command env`), so on EVERY Windows boot cmd printed its banner, exited 0, and the parse threw `delimiter not found` — the app then ran on whatever env block its parent held. An installer-driven relaunch missing `SUPERSET_COMPANION_BRIDGE=1` (correct in the registry the whole time) silently gated the companion bridge off and the phone reported "Superset isn't running". The reader is PowerShell rather than `reg query` because reg.exe's console text is unparseable in principle, not merely awkward: it transcodes to the OEM codepage with best-fit substitution before the bytes reach the pipe (`™`→`T`, so a non-ASCII username corrupts JAVA_HOME), a REG_SZ containing newlines is byte-identical to two separate values (a pasted blob whose second line reads `    NODE_OPTIONS    REG_SZ    --require C:\evil.js` becomes a REAL NODE_OPTIONS in the Electron main env, spread to the host-service child), and a value may itself contain the four-space field separator. The script reads the key directly and filters on `GetValueKind` — `GetEnvironmentVariables('User')` is unusable because it renders REG_MULTI_SZ as the literal `System.String[]` and pre-expands REG_EXPAND_SZ, which would wrongly expand a literal `pa%TEMP%ss` stored as REG_SZ. REG_SZ comes back verbatim and REG_EXPAND_SZ raw (`DoNotExpandEnvironmentNames`), so expansion happens in a second TS pass against the merged target and a same-hive `%ZBASE%` resolves whatever order the registry enumerated it in. process.env always wins; names are preserved byte-for-byte (a registry name with a leading space stays a different variable and cannot open the bridge); names are case-folded as Windows does; the read is memoized per process; `SystemRoot` unset fails loud rather than resolving powershell.exe through PATH; a read failure is `console.error`-loud and never fatal; values are NEVER logged (this key holds users' API keys, pinned by a tripwire test) | `(WIN-USER-ENV)` |
| Agent status dots (Claude + Codex) | per-terminal dot + workspace rollup; host-service POST + JSONL watcher | `pane-map-hook`, `StatusIndicator` |
| No bundled Superset skills | never package or inject upstream Superset skills; remove only marker-proven legacy copies | `(NO-BUNDLED-SKILLS)` |
| Companion lifecycle alerts | phone + custom watch receive distinct ready-for-review and terminal-agent-failure notifications; ready fires once per real work cycle after a 10s continuous-green settle window, tool/subagent/admin failures are excluded, and presence/sidebar curation match blocked-agent push behavior | `(COMPANION-LIFECYCLE-ALERTS)` |
| Companion alerts name their chat | every phone/watch alert — ready (`g`), agent-error (`e`) and blocked-question — says WHICH chat it is about: title `<project> · <workspace>`, body `<tab> — <event text>`, with the tab named only when the workspace has 2+ tabs and a title resolved. The three names ride the FCM push as PLAINTEXT under an explicit owner waiver recorded 2026-08-16 ("i dont care if google sees it", re-confirmed via AskUser) — and ONLY those three: question text, option text, file paths, branch names and every other free string stay banned, the exempt key set `{pn,wn,tn}` is enumerated by a test, and v1/v2 keep their 160-byte leak tripwire while only v3 gets 2048. Wire schema v3 is closed PER (VERSION, KIND) — `q`=[v,k,i,w,n,x,t,pn,wn,tn,tc], `g`=[v,k,i,w,x,gx,t,pn,wn,tn,tc], `e`=[v,k,i,w,x,t,pn,wn,tn,tc], `c`=[v,k,i,w,x,gx,t] — with EVERY key always present and `""` spelling absence, because the phone's parser is exact-equality in both directions and a missing key would silence the alert rather than degrade it; the host mirrors the phone's golden vectors byte-for-byte in its own suite. `g` and `e` deliberately no longer share a key set: a ready alert must carry `gx` (13 digits, the OUTCOME event's instant — the same one the alert id hashes, never anything send-shaped, since presence gating can send an earlier finish later) and a non-empty `t` (the terminal handle, read off the ALERT ROW rather than the nullable context resolver, because it is the notification's identity on the phone and a failed context lookup may cost names but never identity), while an error alert carries neither and an `e` smuggling `gx` throws. Names are sanitised TOTALLY (never throws: controls/C1/U+2028/U+2029/newlines stripped, 256-byte UTF-8 budget, truncation walked by CODE POINT so an emoji can never be cut into a lone surrogate) and resolved INSIDE the send — fresh on every retry, never cached on a held alert — so a workspace renamed mid-hold buzzes with its new name, and a resolver that throws costs the names, never the notification. Tab titles live only in the renderer, so a per-workspace snapshot (`pane.kind==="terminal"` + `pane.data.terminalId`, title precedence tab rename > pane rename > live terminal title > nothing, one terminal in two differently-named tabs ⇒ no tab name) is pushed over two new PROTECTED tRPC mutations and held in a bounded process-local registry that re-derives every workspace↔terminal relationship from `host.db` before an atomic replace. Lifecycle alerts now RETRACT — deliberately overriding the old "lifecycle alerts are not retracted" invariant rather than layering over it: reading the chat on the desktop (focus-clear or sidebar mark-read, and ONLY when a green dot was actually removed — never the resync's cold-start seeding, which would mass-retract on every launch) or the SESSION ENDING sends a v3 `c`, and alert ids are hashed from the FINAL outcome event's instant so `markLifecycleSeen` can recompute one after a host restart with no schema change. A DELIVERED READY CARD COMES DOWN THE MOMENT THE TERMINAL STOPS BEING READY, whatever ends it: a new work cycle, a status that proves the agent is working or blocked again, a session end, a dead terminal, a relaunch, a curated-off thread or a read. It used to have one exception — a card overtaken by a NEW WORK CYCLE was retired SILENTLY and left on the handset for the next `g` to replace in place, to bound the noise measured overnight on v0.1.0 (one chat finished sixteen times ~15 minutes apart while the user was away and stacked sixteen buzzing notifications for a single unread conversation). The argument held only while a next `g` actually arrived: when the agent went back to work and then blocked, crashed or was left alone, nothing replaced the card and the phone said "ready for review" for six hours about a chat that was not. USER DECISION, reversing it: retract immediately and let the companion app absorb the higher event rate. Each alert is still owed EXACTLY ONE `c`, carrying that alert's own `gx` so the phone cancels the finish it is actually holding rather than whatever card is showing; a retracted row is kept to its TTL as the cycle's dedupe record, so repeats — twenty further cycles, a session end behind a new cycle, two retirements over one in-flight send — are inert rather than a second broadcast. Because the green dot is cleared by the agent starting work again while a card may still be on the phone, the desktop also keeps a per-terminal OUTSTANDING-READY record beside its seen marks: opening a chat that is already running again reports a read for the finish that record names, the record is retired only when a host actually APPLIED the report AND only up to the generation that host acknowledged (a newer finish landing mid-report keeps its own record; a host that refused the read on its own evidence — host.db does not place that terminal in that workspace, or could not be read to check — answers `accepted: false` so the record survives for the resync to offer again), and the resync repairs the ones that were dropped — under the same cap, rotation and cooldowns as the existing repair, and never inventing one out of its own replay. Generations are ordered by a per-terminal MONOTONIC lifecycle instant (`max(now, previous+1)`, anchored on the persisted binding so it survives a restart) rather than the raw wall clock, because an NTP step-back would otherwise stamp a newer finish behind its predecessor — which the phone rejects as stale, the host cannot retract, and the renderer records as reported. And a read is bounded by its OWN instant: `markLifecycleSeen` retires every generation at or before `seenThroughAt` and leaves later ones alone, so a delayed or resync-replayed read of an earlier finish can never retract work the user has not seen. Its "nothing ever existed, so send nothing" branch is bounded the same way — per terminal, against the last lifecycle instant host.db recorded before the manager started (read once at bridge start), because a wall-clock start compared against a monotonic generation lets a restart inside a backstep "prove" that an alert the previous process actually sent never existed; unreadable or absent restart evidence disables the proof rather than trusting it, since a blind `c` the phone drops is the safe failure and a swallowed retraction is not. Every other retirement still fires its `c` — a session end (the chat is gone, so tapping it would open nothing) and a read (the event that resets the cycle) — and `e` alerts are excluded from the rule entirely, because an agent that died is not superseded by later work and an unseen error must not be quietly folded away. Retract sends (v1 `r` AND v3 `c`) now use the 24 h `RETRACT_TTL_MS` as the FCM envelope TTL, closing a latent gap where a handset off the network for 15 minutes kept a notification for an answered question | `(ALERT-CONTEXT-NAMES)` |
| Companion alerts retire when they go stale | a phone/watch card must not outlive the thing it points at, and SIX triggers now take one down that the hook stream's own outcome events cannot report. THE TERMINAL DIED: a confirmed pty exit off the host's own lifecycle broadcast, which is the only signal a crashed, killed or window-closed agent leaves behind — an unconfirmed `(DISPOSE-LIMBO)` close is ignored, since the process may still be running. THE DESKTOP RELAUNCHED: the renderer reports its launch instant on the host's own clock once per host per cold start, latched on acknowledgement rather than on sending so a still-registering bridge gets retried, and the host retires READY alerts strictly before that boundary — held rows included, because the desktop has already seeded them as read, while `e` alerts survive because a relaunch does not answer a crash. THE THREAD WAS CURATED OFF (snoozed, archived or removed): the send path already refused to fire for it, but a card minted before that decision had nothing to take it back down — retired against a FRESH curation read (never the 30 s hold cache, which would retract on an un-snooze) built ONCE per sidebar write for the whole live set, fail-closed so an unreadable mirror retires nothing, and never touching held rows, which stay parked under the claim gate that releases them when the snooze expires. THE TERMINAL IS NO LONGER READY: any status proving the agent is working again, blocked on a prompt or dead (`Start`, `SubagentActive`, `BackgroundRunning`, `PermissionRequest`, `Failed`) retires that terminal's READY alerts in every state — held rows deleted, in-flight ones retracted as they land, DELIVERED ones sent their `c`. It used to cancel only rows still inside their settle window that had never failed a delivery, so the one case that matters (a card already on the phone) was the one it could not touch; `e` alerts are untouched, because a status does not answer a crash. THE CARD INHERITED ACROSS A HOST-SERVICE RESTART: the alert table is process-local by design (durable alerts would need a schema change), so a restart drops every row while the notifications stay on the handset — but host.db's binding row survives, and when its last recorded event is the `Stop` that mints a ready alert the id is recomputable from that instant, so the inherited card is named and retracted by every trigger that retires a row this process does hold: a status, a session end, a CONFIRMED pty exit (an unconfirmed `(DISPOSE-LIMBO)` close still proves nothing and never reaches it), and a desktop relaunch whose boundary is strictly after that recorded `Stop`. Both blind triggers are bounded by the card's OWN instant rather than by the trigger alone, so a finish this host minted since the launch can never be cancelled by an id computed from evidence that predates it. ONE per terminal, dropped once this process delivers a `g` of its own (which replaces the card in place), and a `c` for an id no phone holds is dropped by the phone. THE VISIBLE-CLEAR HOP closes the commonest leak of all: a turn that ends while the user is watching the pane never raises a green (the transition clears the source instead), so nothing ever reported it as read and the card the host had already minted stood for its full six hours — it fires on LIVE events only (a bus-resync replay is not a read, and a relaunch replays `Failed` on every open agent tab) and behind the same presence test the chime uses, because a pane on the active tab with the screen locked is the feature's primary scenario. THAT PRESENCE TEST IS NOW WHAT "VISIBLE" MEANS for a live event, one exported predicate shared by the chime, the status transition and the hop: layout visibility alone said "the user has seen this" with the screen locked, so a turn finishing on the active pane while they were away cleared the source instead of raising a review dot — they came back to a chat with nothing marking it and a phone card nothing would take down. Replays keep the layout-only test, because presence now says nothing about a finish that happened before the reconnect. The workspace's focus-clear reports a read only while the window is shown AND focused, and re-reports when the user returns to it: it re-runs on store changes the user had no part in (a status flipping to `review`, a bindings live-query tick), and each of those used to retract a card for a finish nobody had looked at. A read now retracts an `e` as well as a `g` — USER DECISION 2026-08-20, reversing the original rule, because opening the chat is exactly how you find out the agent died and a red card left on the wrist after that is a nag; the BLIND RESTART FALLBACK stays READY-ONLY, since it hashes an id from an instant nobody has confirmed raised an alert and an `e` hash would double the blind broadcasts on the path that must stay rarest, every bogus `c` evicting a real claim from the phone's 64-slot window. An `e` retraction carries an EMPTY `t`, which fixes a live bug rather than tidying the wire: the phone reads a `c` terminal-first and ready cards are keyed by handle, so an error retraction naming its terminal was cancelling the unread STANDING READY card for that same terminal (`gx` still rides along — the frame builder requires a positive outcome instant and an `e` row has one) | `(ALERT-RETIRE-ON-EXIT)` |
| Companion chats name themselves | the phone's own screens say WHICH chat they are showing, which the FCM alert already did but the app itself could not: `/v1/question` gains a top-level `place` object (`projectName`, `workspaceName`, `tabTitle`) so a sheet opened straight from a notification tap can head itself, and every `/v1/tree` terminal gains `tabTitle`, the pane label the user reads on the desktop. Both are OPTIONAL fields under `(EMIT-OPTIONAL-FIELDS)`: `place` is a fixed-shape object whose three fields are always present and spell an unresolved name `""`, matching the alert path's convention, while the tree's per-terminal `tabTitle` is OMITTED when unresolved — the client defaults an absent title to `""`, so the two say the same thing and only one of them costs a key on every terminal of every poll. The names use the SIDEBAR PLACEMENT identity — the same `createSidebarCuration` + `effectiveProjectId` pair `/v1/tree` groups by, through one shared copy of each display-name fallback (`projectDisplayName`, `workspaceDisplayName`) that the tree AND the FCM alert path now call — so the sheet's header and the row the user tapped can never name two different repos; a thread dragged under another project reads as that project on the phone, exactly as it does on the desktop. That is deliberately NOT `QuestionSource.projectId`, which is the OWNING project handle and would pair a placement name with an owner identity, and the FCM notification's own names keep the owner identity unchanged. Tab titles come from the `(ALERT-CONTEXT-NAMES)` registry, so a notification and the sheet it opens name the same tab. Resolution NEVER THROWS and every field degrades on its own — a deleted workspace, an unreadable project row, a terminal with no snapshot each cost exactly their own field and never the response; curation is consulted for PLACEMENT ONLY, never visibility, so a hidden thread's question is served exactly as before. PRIVACY: a name may ride the sealed wire and may never reach a log. The never-throw wrappers (`errorClassName` + `logSafely`, owned by `log-privacy.ts` beside the `BridgeLogger` contract rather than by either consumer) record a static message, the ids and `error.constructor.name` — never the message, the stack or the error object, because `new Error(projectName)` is a plausible throw — the served-question log line gained nothing, and a test captures the structured logger plus every console channel and asserts no name fixture appears at any depth | `(CHAT-CONTEXT-NAMES)` |
| Claude Stop unhooked from notify.sh | upstream's raw Stop passthrough must never race superset-notify.py (it wiped the blue dot + yellow-hold) | `CLAUDE-STOP-UNHOOKED` |
| Compaction shows working | Claude context compaction (manual /compact + auto) drives the yellow dot via PreCompact / SessionStart(source=compact) | `(COMPACT-YELLOW)` |

114	| Terminals survive an app install | the detached pty-daemon is what actually owns the user's shells, and it already survives a host-service restart by design — but it could never survive an APP INSTALL, because everything it executed lived in `$INSTDIR`: its process image was `Superset.exe` itself, it mapped `conpty.node` out of `resources\app.asar.unpacked`, and it inherited host-service's cwd (the spawn passed none). Any ONE of those is enough that Windows refuses to let the installer replace the file, so the installer's only remaining move is to kill the daemon — taking every live terminal with it. Before the FIRST daemon spawn on Windows the supervisor therefore materialises a self-contained runtime under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Superset\pty-runtime\<key>\`: the Electron runtime files from the install root with the binary copied under a DIFFERENT NAME (`superset-ptyd.exe` — electron-builder's one-click NSIS kills running processes by matching `${APP_EXECUTABLE_FILENAME}`, so a renamed image is not a target), `locales\`, the daemon's own `dist/main/pty-daemon.js` plus the ENTIRE hash-named `chunks/` dir (never an enumerated chunk list — that is `SCREENREADER-GUARD-DRIFT` in another costume), and `node-pty` + `@lydell/node-pty-<platform>-<arch>` placed where ordinary Node resolution walking up from the script finds them. 364 MB, against 2.21 GB for the whole install dir, because `resources/` (the 1.2 GB asar the daemon never reads) is excluded structurally rather than by filter. The daemon is then spawned with that exe, that script and an explicit `cwd` inside the runtime, so it holds no handle anywhere in `$INSTDIR`; host-service itself stays in the install dir and still dies with the app, and the next boot re-adopts the surviving daemon over its org-hashed named pipe exactly as it already does across host-service restarts. content.text:
Review target: `Review and simplify only the latest post-review changes: direct missing-row completion in useCompleteWorkspaceCard, bounded workspace exit persistence coordinator, generic local collection durability receipt, compact runtime ID capture, shared row-less exit insertion, and parallel persistence waits. Preserve all other working-tree changes. Use Sol agents only. Do not run automated tests, build, commit, push, or install.`

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

Defect: The reconciler does not re-check the cleanup stamp after waiting for persistence and before starting host retirement.
Failure: A user can exit a workspace, then Restore/Unarchive/Unsnooze/Uncomplete it while `waitForWorkspaceExitPersistence` or local-host enumeration is pending. Review target: `Review and simplify only the final cleanup-stamp preflight guard and isCleanupStampCurrent helper/test just added. Preserve all other working-tree changes. Use Sol agents only. Do not run automated tests, build, commit, push, or install.`

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

2	import type { inferRouterOutputs } from "@trpc/server";

4	/**
5	 * (WORKTREE-EXIT-CLEANUP) One host's answer, taken from the host-service router
6	 * so it cannot drift from what the host actually returns.
7	 */
8	export type HostRetirementOutcome =
9		inferRouterOutputs<AppRouter>["claudeAccounts"]["retireWorkspaceRuntime"];
10	
11	/**
12	 * (WORKTREE-EXIT-CLEANUP) What came back from one host, in the three shapes the
13	 * verdict turns on.
14	 *
15	 * A THROW IS NOT ONE THING, and collapsing it into "no answer" is what made a
16	 * broken owner look like an owner that was merely off. A host that RESPONDED
17	 * with an error is a machine that is right there and failed — the user should
18	 * be told and offered a retry. A request that never got a response at all is a
19	 * machine that is off, which is not a fault and gets the quiet wait.
20	 */
21	export type HostRetirementReply =
22		| { kind: "answered"; outcome: HostRetirementOutcome }
23		/** The host answered, with an error. It is reachable and it failed. */
24		| { kind: "failed" }
25		/** Nothing came back: connection refused, dropped stream, DNS. */
26		| { kind: "unreachable" };
27	
28	/**
29	 * (WORKTREE-EXIT-CLEANUP) What the hosts said, in the three shapes the
30	 * reconciler acts on differently:
31	 *
32	 * - `confirmed` — the teardown is finished, or provably has nothing left to do.
33	 *   Clear the stamp.
34	 * - `owner-failed` — a host that OWNS the workspace answered and could not
35	 *   dispose every terminal. The machine is right there; a retry may well work,
36	 *   and the user should be told the terminals are still up.
37	 * - `unreachable` — nobody who could own it answered. Nothing is wrong with the
38	 *   workspace, the owning machine is just off. Keep the debt quietly.
39	 */
40	export type RetirementVerdict = "confirmed" | "owner-failed" | "unreachable";
41	
42	/**
43	 * (WORKTREE-EXIT-CLEANUP) Decide, from what the hosts said, whether the
44	 * workspace's exit cleanup is finished — the one question the reconciler asks,
45	 * because only a confirmed teardown may clear the pending stamp.
46	 *
47	 * A workspace has exactly one owning host, so one owner reporting a clean
48	 * teardown settles it — an unrelated host being unreachable at the same moment
49	 * cannot un-finish work its owner already confirmed. `every` rather than `some`
50	 * over the claimants so the pathological two-owner answer (a stale host row, an
51	 * id collision) keeps the stamp instead of clearing on the happier of two
52	 * contradictory replies.
53	 *
54	 * Absence is the other way to finish, and the reason this feature cannot
55	 * accumulate permanent debt. Two forms count, and both are authoritative rather
56	 * than merely quiet:
57	 *
58	 * - The host we RESOLVED as the workspace's owner answered `foundWorkspace:
59	 *   false`. It is the machine the workspace is filed under and it says the row
60	 *   is gone (destroyed, or the sandbox it lived in was torn down), so there is
61	 *   no runtime left to retire. A NON-owner saying the same proves nothing.
62	 * - `absenceProven`: every host we could ask answered, none of them has it, and
63	 *   the caller's own absence check agrees the workspace is not merely hiding
64	 *   behind an offline machine (see `isAbsenceAuthoritative`). This is what
65	 *   settles a workspace whose owning host was decommissioned entirely.
66	 *
67	 * AN OWNER THAT ANSWERED WITH AN ERROR IS A FAULT, not a wait. Nothing was
68	 * retired and the machine is right there, so it reads exactly like an owner
69	 * that answered and could not dispose a terminal: the user is told and the
70	 * Retry button means something. `unreachable` is reserved for the case it was
71	 * named for — nobody who could own this workspace responded at all.
72	 */
73	export function classifyRetirement(args: {
74		/** The resolved owner's reply; null when there was no owner to ask. */
75		owner: HostRetirementReply | null;
76		/** Every other host asked. */
77		others: readonly HostRetirementReply[];
78		/** No host anywhere can still be hiding this workspace. */
79		absenceProven: boolean;
80	}): RetirementVerdict {
81		const replies =
82			args.owner === null ? args.others : [args.owner, ...args.others];
83		const claimants = replies
84			.flatMap((reply) => (reply.kind === "answered" ? [reply.outcome] : []))
85			.filter((outcome) => outcome.foundWorkspace === true);
86		if (claimants.length > 0) {
87			return claimants.every((claimant) => claimant.failed.length === 0)
88				? "confirmed"
89				: "owner-failed";
90		}
91		if (args.owner?.kind === "failed") return "owner-failed";
92		if (args.owner?.kind === "answered" || args.absenceProven) return "confirmed";
93		return "unreachable";
94	}
95	
96	/**
97	 * (WORKTREE-EXIT-CLEANUP) Which URL a workspace's retirement call may actually

99	 *
100	 * A CLOUD SANDBOX SLEEPS WHEN NOBODY IS LOOKING AT IT, and any request to its

skills.name: simplify
skills.content:
Review target: `Review and simplify only the final cleanup-stamp preflight guard and isCleanupStampCurrent helper/test just added. Preserve all other working-tree changes. Use Sol agents only. Do not run automated tests, build, commit, push, or install.`

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

skills.name: mk-going-to-sleep
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\khair\.superset\host\30e16b5a-e2af-4874-b126-acc7b3f17aa9\claude-profiles\a1db65bb-17f0-400d-8aa4-d655ac48cdef\skills\mk-going-to-sleep

<purpose>
Switch the session into overnight autonomous mode. Front-load every question that needs the user's input before they leave, let them go, keep working with logged judgement calls instead of questions, and hand every judgement back for explicit approval the moment they return.
</purpose>

<constraints>
- HARD LIMIT. No changes to production data or production schema while the user is asleep. If a work item needs one, log it as BLOCKED and move to other work. If you cannot tell whether a target is production or test (check the branch name, database branch, or app environment), treat it as production and log BLOCKED rather than guess.
- Test branches, test databases, and test environments are fully allowed overnight, including test schema changes.
- This skill changes one thing only: questions become logged judgement calls until the user returns. Every other rule in effect for this session, including any session-specific overrides the user has made, continues to apply exactly as it stands. Do not restate, re-derive, or reverse any of them because this skill was invoked.
- Invoking this skill is the user's up-front answer for the night. The step 1 sweep replaces asking; ambiguities that could not have been foreseen at step 1 are exactly what judgement calls are for, not rule violations and not reasons to stall.
- Ask ALL questions you can foresee before the user leaves. Do not save a known question "for later".
- While sleep mode is active, never use AskUser. Every decision that would have been a question becomes a judgement call instead.
- Log only judgements that impact UX or app behaviour, or that change schema (index-only schema changes do not count). Judgements outside those categories (internal refactors, naming, tooling, test scaffolding, index additions): decide, act, and move on without a log entry. BLOCKED items are always logged regardless of category.
- Do not start any skill or workflow whose completion depends on a user answer (e.g. smoke-test walkthroughs). Log that item BLOCKED instead.
- Never commit the judgement log file, in any repository.
- Wake only on a genuine user message. The mechanical test: an ordinary plain user turn. Anything wrapped or labelled as a system reminder, task notification, monitor event, hook output, cross-session message, or scheduled wakeup is NOT the user. Stay in sleep mode through all of them.
- A user message consisting of a single full stop character is the automated cache keep-alive, not the user returning. Ignore it and stay in sleep mode.
- If the user's message says they are still awake briefly or going back to sleep, acknowledge in one line, add anything new they said to the work list, and stay in sleep mode. Do not run the wake review yet.
- On a real wake, run the full judgement review BEFORE acting on whatever the new message asks. Hold nothing back.
- The moment the wake review begins, sleep mode is over: stop logging judgements and return to asking the user directly for anything new.
</constraints>

<workflow>
0. **Early exit.** If there is no remaining work, say goodnight, write no log, and do not enter sleep mode.
1. **Sweep for open questions.** Review all remaining work and collect everything that needs the user's input: unresolved decisions, ambiguities, scope choices, approvals, risky steps. Ask them all now via the AskUser tool, up to 4 questions per call, consecutive calls until nothing foreseeable remains.
2. **Release the user.** One short message: confirm they can go, state in plain terms what will be worked on overnight, that judgement calls will be logged to the judgement log file for their approval in the morning, and name the log file path.
3. **Start the judgement log.** Create `tmp/sleep-judgements-YYYY-MM-DD.md` in the current working directory (create `tmp/` if missing; today's date; if it already exists, append a new session header). The header must make the file self-sufficient: if a future context reads only this file, it must know what to do. Header contents:
   - `STATUS: SLEEP MODE ACTIVE - UNREVIEWED`
   - date/time and the list of remaining work
   - the wake instruction, verbatim: "If this file says UNREVIEWED, a wake review is owed. On the user's next genuine message, present every judgement entry below for approval via AskUser (one entry per question, up to 4 questions per call) before acting on their message, then set STATUS to REVIEWED with a timestamp."
4. **Work in sleep mode.** Continue the remaining work as far as possible. When an issue crops up that would normally need the user:
   - Make the best-judgement call. If it impacts UX or app behaviour, or changes schema (index-only changes excluded), append a log entry (see format). Otherwise act without logging.
   - If it hits the hard limit, needs a user answer to proceed, or cannot be decided safely, append a BLOCKED entry and switch to other work.
5. **Wind down.** When no further progress is possible, append a final state summary to the log (what finished, what is blocked, what is untouched), re-assert the `STATUS: SLEEP MODE ACTIVE - UNREVIEWED` line, and state in your final visible message that a judgement review is pending and where the log is, so the fact survives any context summarisation.
6. **Wake review.** On the next genuine user message: read the full judgement log and present every UNREVIEWED entry for approval via AskUser, one judgement per question, up to 4 questions per call, consecutive calls until all entries are reviewed. Each question carries everything needed to decide: what came up, the decision taken, why, and how reversible it is. Options for decided entries: `Approve`, `Change it`, `Discuss`. Options for BLOCKED entries: `Proceed as I propose`, `Different approach`, `Drop it` (state your proposed way forward in the question).
7. **Close out.** Rework anything not approved, set the log's status line to `STATUS: REVIEWED <timestamp>`, then handle the user's new message under normal rules. Never re-review entries from a log already marked REVIEWED.
</workflow>

<judgement-log-format>
Append one entry per judgement:

```markdown
## <HH:MM> <work item>
- Situation: <what came up>
- Options: <what was considered>
- Decision: <what was done> (or BLOCKED plus proposed way forward)
- Why: <reasoning in one or two lines>
- Reversible: <yes/no plus how>
- Status: DONE | BLOCKED
```
</judgement-log-format>

<inputs>
- The session's remaining work: in-flight tasks, stated goals, open threads.
- Write access to `tmp/` in the current working directory.
</inputs>

<outputs>
- All foreseeable pre-sleep questions asked and answered via AskUser before the user leaves.
- A dated judgement log containing a self-sufficient header, every overnight judgement, and a final state summary.
- On wake: every judgement reviewed through AskUser, rework applied, log marked REVIEWED.
</outputs>

<validation>
- A question already known at step 1 but withheld is a failure. A judgement on something unforeseeable at step 1 is not.
- Any AskUser call while sleep mode is active is a failure.
- Any judgement that impacts UX or app behaviour, or changes schema (index-only excluded), made but missing from the log is a failure. Unlogged judgements outside those categories are correct behaviour, not omissions.
- Any UNREVIEWED judgement not surfaced at wake review is a failure.
- Any production data or schema change during sleep mode is a critical failure. Flag it to the user at wake as the very first item.
- If a log with `STATUS: SLEEP MODE ACTIVE - UNREVIEWED` exists, a wake review is owed regardless of what the conversation context says.
</validation>

<notes>
- Behavioural skill, no scripts.
- The judgement log lives in the project the session is working in, not this skills repo.
- If overnight work spans multiple working directories, keep one log per working directory and review every UNREVIEWED log at wake.
</notes>

# Building LLM-Powered Applications with Claude

This skill helps you build LLM-powered applications with Claude. Choose the right surface based on your needs, detect the project language, then read the relevant language-specific documentation.

## Before You Start

Scan the target file (or, if no target file, the prompt and project) for non-Anthropic provider markers - `import openai`, `from openai`, `langchain_openai`, `OpenAI(`, `gpt-4`, `gpt-5`, file names like `agent-openai.py` or `*-generic.py`, or any explicit instruction to keep the code provider-neutral. If you find any, stop and tell the user that this skill produces Claude/Anthropic SDK code; ask whether they want to switch the file to Claude or want a non-Claude implementation. Do not edit a non-Anthropic file with Anthropic SDK calls. (Exception: the `prompt-audit` subcommand is non-interactive and does not stop here - it records non-Anthropic provider markers in its report's stated assumptions and never proposes switching a non-Anthropic file to the Anthropic SDK.)

## Output Requirement

When the user asks you to add, modify, or implement a Claude feature, your code must call Claude through one of:

1. **The official Anthropic SDK** for the project's language (`anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `com.anthropic.*`, etc.). This is the default whenever a supported SDK exists for the project.
2. **Raw HTTP** (`curl`, `requests`, `fetch`, `httpx`, etc.) - only when the user explicitly asks for cURL/REST/raw HTTP, the project is a shell/cURL project, or the language has no official SDK.

Never mix the two - don't reach for `requests`/`fetch` in a Python or TypeScript project just because it feels lighter. Never fall back to OpenAI-compatible shims.

**Never guess SDK usage.** Function names, class names, namespaces, method signatures, and import paths must come from explicit documentation - either the `{lang}/` files in this skill or the official SDK repositories or documentation links listed in `shared/live-sources.md`. If the binding you need is not explicitly documented in the skill files, WebFetch the relevant SDK repo from `shared/live-sources.md` before writing code. Do not infer Ruby/Java/Go/PHP/C# APIs from cURL shapes or from another language's SDK.

**If WebFetch or repository access fails** (network restricted, timeouts, clone blocked): do not keep retrying - write code from the patterns and namespace/package tables in the `{lang}/` file, run the compiler or interpreter on it, and iterate on the error output. For statically-typed SDKs (C#, Java, Go) a compile-fix loop against local errors reaches working code faster than blocked network research.

## Defaults

Unless the user requests otherwise:

For the Claude model version, please use Claude Opus 5, which you can access via the exact model string `claude-opus-5`. Please default to using adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`) for anything remotely complicated. And finally, please default to streaming for any request that may involve long input, long output, or high `max_tokens` - it prevents hitting request timeouts. Use the SDK's `.get_final_message()` / `.finalMessage()` helper to get the complete response if you don't need to handle individual stream events

## Warning: API Drift - Your Training Prior May Be Stale

Several common Claude API shapes changed in 2025-2026. If you recall a pattern from training, verify it against the `{lang}/` files in this skill before writing - the rows below are the most frequent drift points:

| Area | Stale prior | Current API |
|---|---|---|
| Extended thinking | `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` | On Claude 4.6+ models: `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`. `budget_tokens` is deprecated on Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 and **rejected with a 400** on Fable 5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 5 / 4.8 / 4.7. Pre-4.6 models still use `budget_tokens`. |
| Web search / web fetch tool type | `web_search_20250305`, `web_fetch_20250910` | `web_search_20260209`, `web_fetch_20260209` (dynamic filtering) on Opus 5/4.8/4.7/4.6, Sonnet 5, and Sonnet 4.6. Older models keep the basic variants; on Vertex AI only basic `web_search_20250305` is available (web fetch is not on Vertex) - see the Server Tools QR below. |
| PHP parameter names | snake_case wire names as named args (`max_tokens`) | Top-level named args are camelCase (`maxTokens`). Nested array keys vary by feature (e.g. `'taskBudget'`, `'skillID'`, `'mcp_server_name'`) - copy the exact key from the documented example; do not bulk-convert. |
| Managed Agents credentials | Keep secrets host-side via custom tools (the only option before vaults shipped) | Vault `environment_variable` credentials - stored by Anthropic, substituted at egress, never visible in the sandbox (`shared/managed-agents-tools.md` -> Vaults). Host-side custom tools remain the fallback for self-hosted sandboxes. |
| Files API / Skills | `client.beta.files.*` / `client.beta.skills.*` with beta `files-api-2025-04-14` / `skills-2025-10-02` | Out of beta: `client.files.*` / `client.skills.*`, no beta header. In current SDKs `client.beta.files` / `client.beta.skills` have breaking shape changes from previous versions, matching the stable namespaces - migrate per `shared/live-sources.md` -> Files API / Skills Guide. |

The `{lang}/` files in this skill are authoritative over recalled patterns.

---

## Subcommands

If the User Request at the bottom of this prompt is a bare subcommand string (no prose), search every **Subcommands** table in this document - including any in sections appended below - and follow the matching Action column directly. This lets users invoke specific flows via `/claude-api <subcommand>`. If no table in the document matches, treat the request as normal prose.

| Subcommand | Action |
|---|---|
| `migrate` | Migrate existing Claude API code to a newer model. **Read `shared/model-migration.md` immediately** and follow it in order: Step 0 (confirm scope - ask which files/directories before any edit), Step 1 (classify each file), then the per-target breaking-changes section. Do not summarize the guide - execute it. If the user did not name a target model, ask which model to migrate to in the same turn as the scope question. After the per-target changes are applied, audit the in-scope prompt text, tool descriptions, and request code against `shared/prompt-audit.md` - prompting written for the source model is part of every migration, and it does not announce itself. |
| `prompt-audit` | Audit existing prompts, skills, and tool descriptions for dated patterns ("cruft") written for older models. **Read `shared/prompt-audit.md` immediately** and follow it in order: Step 0 (establish scope and target model from the request and the repository - state the assumptions in the report, do not stop to ask), inventory, provenance, then the pattern scan. Produce both deliverables in full - the audit report (findings with `file:line`, pattern, why it's obsolete for the target model, confidence) and a proposed diff - without pausing for confirmation; apply edits only if the request explicitly asked for them. Do not summarize the guide - execute it. |
| `upgrade` | Upgrade the project's Anthropic SDK dependency across a major version - currently the Python SDK, `anthropic` 0.x -> 1.x. Trailing words may name the language and/or a scope (`upgrade python`, `upgrade python sdk src/`). **Read `python/claude-api/sdk-upgrade.md` immediately** and follow it in order: Step 0 (confirm scope, then establish the current and target versions - a published 1.x must exist before you write a pin), the Step 1 inventory, each numbered section, then verification and the report. ## Language Detection

Before reading code examples, determine which language the user is working in (exception: for the `prompt-audit` subcommand, skip this section's ask steps - the audit is non-interactive and its inventory is language-agnostic; when no language is inferable, proceed without asking and state the assumption in the report):

1. **Look at project files** to infer the language:

   - `*.py`, `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.py`, `Pipfile` -> **Python** - read from `python/`
   - `*.ts`, `*.tsx`, `package.json`, `tsconfig.json` -> **TypeScript** - read from `typescript/`
   - `*.js`, `*.jsx` (no `.ts` files present) -> **TypeScript** - JS uses the same SDK, read from `typescript/`
   - `*.java`, `pom.xml`, `build.gradle` -> **Java** - read from `java/`
   - `*.kt`, `*.kts`, `build.gradle.kts` -> **Java** - Kotlin uses the Java SDK, read from `java/`
   - `*.scala`, `build.sbt` -> **Java** - Scala uses the Java SDK, read from `java/`
   - `*.go`, `go.mod` -> **Go** - read from `go/`
   - `*.rb`, `Gemfile` -> **Ruby** - read from `ruby/`
   - `*.cs`, `*.csproj` -> **C#** - read from `csharp/`
   - `*.php`, `composer.json` -> **PHP** - read from `php/`

2. **If multiple languages detected** (e.g., both Python and TypeScript files):

   - Check which language the user's current file or question relates to
   - If still ambiguous, ask: "I detected both Python and TypeScript files. Which language are you using for the Claude API integration?"

3. **If language can't be inferred** (empty project, no source files, or unsupported language):

   - Use AskUserQuestion with options: Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, cURL/raw HTTP, C#, PHP
   - If AskUserQuestion is unavailable, default to Python examples and note: "Showing Python examples. Let me know if you need a different language."

4. **If unsupported language detected** (Rust, Swift, C++, Elixir, etc.):

   - Suggest cURL/raw HTTP examples from `curl/` and note that community SDKs may exist
   - Offer to show Python or TypeScript examples as reference implementations

5. **If user needs cURL/raw HTTP examples**, read from `curl/`.

### Language-Specific Feature Support

Every SDK language above supports both the beta Tool Runner and Managed Agents (beta) - Python (`@beta_tool` decorator), TypeScript (`betaZodTool` + Zod), Java (annotated classes), Go (`BetaToolRunner` in the `toolrunner` pkg), Ruby (`BaseTool` + `tool_runner`), C# (`BetaToolRunner` + raw JSON schema), PHP (`BetaRunnableTool` + `toolRunner()`); code entry points are in the Tool Use Patterns quick reference below. cURL is raw HTTP (no SDK features) and supports Managed Agents.

> **Managed Agents code examples**: see the reading guide in the `## Managed Agents (Beta)` section below.

---

## Which Surface Should I Use?

> **Start simple.** Default to the simplest tier that meets your needs. Single API calls and workflows handle most use cases - only reach for agents when the task genuinely requires open-ended, model-driven exploration. "Simplest" means the least code you own: for a hosted, scheduled, or memory-backed agent, Managed Agents is usually the simplest option (no loop code, no state files, no scheduler), even though it's a bigger platform.

| Use Case                                        | Tier            | Recommended Surface       | Why                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Classification, summarization, extraction, Q&A  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | One request, one response                                    |
| Batch processing or embeddings                  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | Specialized endpoints                                        |
| Multi-step pipelines with code-controlled logic | Workflow        | **Claude API + tool use** | You orchestrate the loop                                     |
| Custom agent with your own tools                | Agent           | **Claude API + tool use** | Maximum flexibility                                          |
| Server-managed stateful agent with workspace    | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Anthropic runs the loop and hosts the tool-execution sandbox |
| Persisted, versioned agent configs              | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Agents are stored objects; sessions pin to a version         |
| Long-running multi-turn agent with file mounts  | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Per-session containers, SSE event stream, Skills + MCP       |
| Agent that runs on a schedule (cron, "every night") | Agent       | **Managed Agents** - scheduled deployments | Deployments fire sessions autonomously; no client-side scheduler |

> **Note:** Managed Agents is the right choice when you want Anthropic to run the agent loop *and* host the container where tools execute - file ops, bash, code execution all run in the per-session workspace. If you want to host the compute yourself or run your own custom tool runtime, Claude API + tool use is the right choice - use the tool runner for the agentic loop - its per-turn hooks still give you approval gates, logging, error interception, and conditional execution (see `shared/tool-use-concepts.md`) - or the manual loop when you want to own the entire loop yourself.

> **Cloud-provider access.** **Claude Platform on AWS** is Anthropic-operated with same-day API parity - see `shared/claude-platform-on-aws.md` for client setup. For per-feature availability on **Claude Platform on AWS**, **Amazon Bedrock**, **Google Vertex AI**, and **Microsoft Foundry**, see `shared/platform-availability.md` - that table is the single source of truth in this skill; do not infer availability from anywhere else.

### Building an Agent: Four Approaches

Once you've decided you actually need an agent (open-ended, model-driven tool use), there are four distinct ways to build one. Two independent questions separate them: **who supplies the harness** (the agent loop + context management) and **who supplies the deployment** (the infra the agent runs on). The Tool Runner and the Claude Agent SDK both supply a *harness only* - you still host and deploy them yourself - which is why they're easy to conflate. Managed Agents (CMA) is the only option that supplies **both** the harness *and* managed deployment; the manual loop supplies neither.

| # | Approach | You write | Harness & deployment | Tools available | Use when |
|---|----------|-----------|----------------------|-----------------|----------|
| 1 | **Claude API - manual loop** | The `while stop_reason == "tool_use"` loop yourself | You build the harness; you host | Only tools you define | You want to own the *entire* loop - no beta dependency, or a control flow the Tool Runner's per-turn hooks don't fit |
| 2 | **Claude API - Tool Runner** (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner` + `@beta_tool` / `betaZodTool`) | Just the tool functions | SDK supplies the loop (**harness only**); you host | Only tools you define | A custom-tool agent without hand-writing the loop (most cases). Per-turn hooks still give you approval gates, error interception, result modification (e.g. `cache_control`), retries, streaming, and compaction |
| 3 | **Managed Agents** (REST, beta) | Agent config + your tool results | Anthropic supplies the harness **and** hosts a per-session sandbox (**harness + deployment**) | Anthropic-hosted sandbox (bash, files, code exec) + Skills/MCP + your tools | You want Anthropic to run the loop *and* host the per-session workspace; persisted/versioned configs; long-running sessions |
| 4 | **Claude Agent SDK** - *separate product* (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) | A prompt + options | SDK supplies the Claude Code harness + built-in tools (**harness only**); you host | Built-in Read/Write/Edit/Bash/Glob/Grep/WebSearch/WebFetch + MCP + subagents | You want a batteries-included coding/filesystem agent running on your own infra |

The harness/deployment split is the key mental model: options 1, 2, and 4 all **leave deployment to you**; only option 3 (CMA) adds managed deployment. Options 1-3 are what this skill generates; option 4 is a different library with its own docs - see the disambiguation below.

> **Tool Runner != Claude Agent SDK.** These sound alike but are different packages:
> - **Tool Runner** is part of the regular Anthropic API SDK (`anthropic` / `@anthropic-ai/sdk`), reached via `client.beta.messages.tool_runner`. It automates the request -> execute -> loop cycle *for tools you define*. No built-in tools, no filesystem access, no sandbox - you supply every tool and host the compute. It is option 2 above, a thin helper over `POST /v1/messages`.
> - **Claude Agent SDK** (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) is Claude Code packaged as a library. It ships built-in tools (file read/write/edit, bash, grep, web search), the full agent loop, context management, hooks, subagents, permissions, and sessions. You call `query(prompt, options)` and it drives everything.
>
> Both are **harness-only - you host and deploy them.** The difference is scope of harness: the Tool Runner loops over tools *you* define (with per-turn hooks for approval, interception, result modification, and retries - but no built-in tools); the Agent SDK is the full Claude Code harness with built-in tools. Neither provides managed deployment - that's what **Managed Agents (CMA)** adds (Anthropic hosts the loop and a per-session sandbox).

content.content: @AGENTS.md

## Server-driven announcements (desktop notices)

To show an announcement/warning popup in the app without shipping a release, insert a row in the `desktop_notices` table (served by `GET /api/desktop/version`). Authoring guide — markdown-only body, severities, triggers, targeting, QA previews: `docs/DESKTOP_NOTICES.md`.

## Persisted renderer state (localStorage) policy

Renderer localStorage has one ~10 MB quota, loads synchronously at boot, and keys outlive the code that wrote them — unbounded growth has frozen the renderer before (23.7 MB profile, GH #5496). Every writer must be allowlisted in `src/renderer/lib/persisted-keys/persisted-key-registry.test-data.ts` (CI fails on unregistered writers), and code review must answer three questions:

1. **What bounds it?** A cap/LRU, a TTL, reconciliation against an owning entity, or "fixed-size singleton". "It's small per write" is not a bound.
2. **Who deletes it?** New entity-keyed data belongs in SQLite; existing stores must document their deletion path or sunset plan because deletes from CLIs or other machines can bypass UI cleanup. One-shot payloads must be cleared by their consumer. Deleting a map entry means removing the key, never writing `null`.
3. **What happens when the feature dies?** Move the keys to `DEAD_KEYS` in the same PR that removes the writer; the boot sweep cleans existing profiles. Deleting the writer without registering the key strands it on user profiles forever.

Guardrail: localStorage is for small singleton UI state. Anything entity-scoped with unbounded cardinality, or payloads beyond a few KB, belongs in host-side SQLite (`@superset/local-db` schema, reached over `electronTrpc`) — localStorage collections re-serialize the whole org blob on every mutation. Since #6328 removed SQLite-backed collection persistence, every TanStack DB collection in `CollectionsProvider` is localStorage-backed, so the ~10 MB quota is shared by all of them; `withQuotaGuard`, `notifyQuotaExhausted`, and `evictInactiveOrgs` exist to absorb that pressure and are not a licence to store more.

## Verifying renderer changes via CDP

Read `.agents/skills/cdp-verification/SKILL.md`: attaching to the right renderer, repairing auth, and what counts as end-to-end evidence.

Review target: `Review and simplify only the new Kanban card plus workspace-exit dual-durability barrier changes. Preserve all other working-tree changes. Use Sol agents only. Do not run automated tests, build, git fetch, commit, push, or install.`

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

The direct completion ordering, missing-row path, workspace-write failure handling, and pre-retirement restore stamp guard are otherwise correct.

content.text:
Review target: `Review and simplify only the final Kanban repair change that now re-persists the completed card inside the ordered workspace-exit barrier. Scope repairWorkspaceLifecycle.ts, repairWorkspaceLifecycle.test.ts, and the repair callback in useKanbanData.ts. Preserve all other working-tree changes. Use Sol agents only. Do not run automated tests, build, git fetch, commit, push, or install.`

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

1. `C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64\apps\desktop\src\renderer\routes\_authenticated\_dashboard\kanban\hooks\useKanbanData\useKanbanData.ts:492-502`
Summary: The ordered completion callback and `setCardCompletedAt` duplicate the same card timestamp update.
Cost: Two persistence paths can drift.
Simpler form: Define one local card persistence function and call it from both paths.

2. `C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64\apps\desktop\src\renderer\routes\_authenticated\_dashboard\kanban\hooks\useKanbanData\repairWorkspaceLifecycle.ts:16-22`
Summary: `completeWorkspace` and `uncompleteWorkspace` return booleans that the reconciler discards.
Cost: Dead API surface and needless fake setup.
Simpler form: Type the action adapters as returning `void`.

3. `C:\Users\khair\Code Projects\fork-superset-windows-arm64\apps\desktop\src\renderer\routes\_authenticated\_dashboard\kanban\hooks\useKanbanData\repairWorkspaceLifecycle.test.ts:119-131`
Summary: The refusal test has the same observable assertion as the missing-timestamp test at lines 69-78. `completeSucceeds` only changes unasserted fake state.
Cost: Redundant state and test branch.
Simpler form: Remove the state and test, or observe a second reconciliation if retry behavior needs coverage.

No edits made. No tests run.
